question: A patient sustains an ulnar nerve injury at the wrist. Compared with an ulnar nerve injury at the elbow, the wrist-level injury produces a MORE severe claw hand deformity. Which mechanism BEST explains this 'ulnar paradox'?

answers.text: Wrist-level injuries also damage the median nerve, adding thenar weakness to claw deformity.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The ulnar paradox is a property of the ulnar nerve alone and does not involve co-injury of the median nerve. The explanation lies in the intact versus denervated flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) contribution.

answers.text: At wrist level, the flexor digitorum profundus to the ring and little fingers is intact (innervated proximally), so unopposed FDP pull accentuates IP flexion, worsening the claw.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The ulnar nerve supplies FDP to the ring and little fingers via a branch in the forearm, proximal to the wrist. A wrist-level injury spares this branch, leaving FDP intact and powerful. With intrinsic (lumbrical + interossei) loss, FDP pulls the IPs into full flexion without opposition, producing a severe claw. At elbow level, FDP is also denervated, so the claw is less pronounced despite higher injury.

answers.text: Wrist-level injuries always involve neurotmesis while elbow-level injuries are usually axonotmesis, accounting for the difference in severity.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The ulnar paradox is an anatomical phenomenon related to the level of FDP innervation, not to the histological type of injury. Severity of claw is the same regardless of whether the injury is axonotmesis or neurotmesis at either level.

answers.text: At wrist level, the hypothenar muscles are spared, reducing overall deformity compared with elbow-level injuries.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the opposite of the paradox. At wrist level, the hypothenar muscles are denervated (their motor branch arises from the ulnar nerve in the Guyon canal, distal to a wrist laceration), and the claw is MORE severe, not less.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key is the FDP branch origin: in the forearm, proximal to the wrist. Wrist injury = FDP intact + intrinsics lost = severe claw (paradoxically worse than elbow injury).
Excellent. The ulnar paradox: wrist injury spares FDP (forearm branch intact) → unopposed FDP pull → severe claw. Elbow injury denervates FDP too → less claw despite higher injury.
